content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In Christian teaching, grass primarily symbolizes the transience, frailty, and mortality of human life — the brevity of human existence and glory in contrast to the eternal, unchanging word and nature of God. Humanity 'is like grass' that flourishes briefly, then withers and is gone.", "primary_basis": ["Isaiah 40:6-8 ('All flesh is grass... the grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God stands forever')", "Psalm 103:15-16 ('As for man, his days are like grass...')", "Psalm 90:5-6 ('in the morning it flourishes... in the evening it fades and withers')", "1 Peter 1:24-25 (quoting Isaiah 40 to contrast perishable flesh with the enduring word)", "James 1:10-11 (the rich man will fade away 'like a flower of the grass')", "Psalm 37:2 (evildoers 'will soon fade like the grass')", "Job 8:12; Job 14:2 (human life withering like plants)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "God's providential care and provision: grass as something God feeds, waters, and clothes, used to argue from lesser to greater that God will care for his people (and, in pastoral imagery, as a picture of divine sustenance and rest).", "basis": ["Matthew 6:30 / Luke 12:28 ('if God so clothes the grass of the field...')", "Psalm 104:14 ('You cause the grass to grow for the livestock')", "Psalm 23:2 ('He makes me lie down in green pastures')", "Deuteronomy 11:15"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "The fleeting prosperity of the wicked: the wicked sprout and flourish like grass only to be swiftly destroyed, a subset of the transience theme applied specifically to God's enemies.", "basis": ["Psalm 92:7 ('though the wicked sprout like grass... they are doomed to destruction forever')", "Psalm 37:1-2", "Psalm 129:6 (like grass on housetops that withers before it grows up)", "2 Kings 19:26 / Isaiah 37:27"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Abundance, fruitfulness, or multitude: grass as an image of numerous offspring or flourishing blessing.", "basis": ["Job 5:25 ('your descendants... like the grass of the earth')", "Psalm 72:16 (people flourishing 'like grass of the field')", "Isaiah 44:4 ('they shall spring up among the grass')"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "In apocalyptic interpretation, the grass of Revelation is sometimes read symbolically as people or humanity (drawing on the 'all flesh is grass' motif), so that the burning or sparing of grass represents judgment on human beings; most commentators, however, treat it as literal vegetation.", "basis": ["Revelation 8:7 (a third of the grass burned up)", "Revelation 9:4 (locusts told not to harm the grass)", "Isaiah 40:6-7 as interpretive background"], "prominence": "minority"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is a strong, widely recognized consensus across Protestant, Catholic, and Orthodox commentary that grass is the Bible's standard image for the brevity and frailty of mortal human life, anchored above all in Isaiah 40:6-8 and its New Testament citation in 1 Peter 1:24-25. The alternative senses (divine provision, the short-lived wicked, abundance) are well attested in Scripture and commentary but are generally treated as contextual uses rather than rivals to the primary symbolism. The symbolic 'grass = people' reading in Revelation exists mainly in some popular and dispensational or idealist commentary and is not the majority scholarly view."}
